blocks.x: What was your right name?
Well, I was born into the Smith clan. My name is Richard, and to make me different, they decided to name me Richard Charles Howard Smith. A lot of relatives got in the act there.
Well, that would be good for a trumpet player. You know, you get the Howard in there.

Some people like that. Let's talk about Kid Ory. Kid Ory, to me, now we're premising this on the fact that I did play in his band on his pickup gigs and on weekends during the period of about 1958 through 1960. Maybe there was some in 57. I don't know. I recall the George Lewis band at that time, though, in San Francisco. But my early recollections were Ory on Records, of course, those wonderful crescents that came out of Los Angeles, swinging things with Mutt Carey and Bud Scott, and then as I got in college, I used to follow the Ory band. I think nothing of driving 40, 50 miles to catch him at some remote beach resort, playing in some remote ballroom that had the stench of faded gardenias still in it. And I'd hear great people like Bud Scott in his day, and he was a charming mountain of a man who really played. And the band swung, and it was very cohesive, very enjoyable. I remember Buster Wilson, the piano player, doing things like River of the Roses, these wonderful old pop tunes that they would just swing in a very, what I felt was a very polished and wonderful New Orleans style. And then fortunes took me all around, and as I got back to San Francisco, the magic of circumstance brought me in touch with Ory, and he needed a trumpet player, and I was playing a little trumpet at that time. I certainly had my ears hanging out and was listening to his style well enough that I could just step right in and play pretty well. I understood the ensemble playing. I never considered myself a virtuoso soloist. In fact, nobody in Ory's band really specialized in that kind of thing. It was a good, cohesive ensemble band. And I think he was properly named Kidd, if I understand the traditions of that nomenclature. He was a bit of a dude, and he always had a little flash to him, snappy dresser, and he certainly did respond to a crowd, and they responded to him. And he was a strong, strong character. He, as a musician, he had certain little patterns built in. The opener every night was Sheik of Araby. We just automatically, without saying a word, we'd just get up on the stand, and his foot was, you know, he laid with his foot. You know, he'd stomp two times, and we were playing the Sheik of Araby. He'd play the lead. That would loosen him up, and the clarinet and I would be playing the little badadadadadud riffs in the back kind of thing. And by the time the last chorus was going, all the blood was flowing to the lips, and we were ready to play just about anything. And he played a pretty good variety of the things that he's known for on his records. Did he? He liked to play, because Louis had had such a good success with it, he liked to play that song, and this is Ori's words, Max the Knife. Loved to play Max the Knife.
Did he have a theme song then, really?

Well, yeah, usually on a sentimental Saturday night, after we were, you know, we'd accept a drink or two from the audience long about late in the evening, and when we had the rapport going, and the audience was really rolling, and having a good time, and we were having a good time, and it was the last set. We'd always ended up with his theme song, which was, I never understood it way back in those college days when I heard him play it, but it's just an old pop tune he was fond of called Without You, For an Inspiration, Dear. And it had some words that went to it. I don't know where I heard these, but they stuck in my mind. They're inspirational poetry. No bird would ever sing, no bell would ever ring, Without you, for an inspiration, dear. And it went on and it got worse after that. It was pretty sticky. It's just a syrupy pop tune from I have no idea what period in Ori's life, or I have no idea who he was in love with at the time that might have prompted him to be so fond of it.
Well, he probably didn't have many women in his life, I don't think.
I don't keep score of things like that.
No, who could?
No, he struck me as... After all, he was about 75 when I was playing with him. Yeah. I think he was tapering off.
Well, when I met him was that.
I planned to taper off about that age.
But when I met him, he still struck me. And he was still a handsome, personable guy, even though he was old and weak. Definitely.

I would call it... He had a lot of sparkle. You know, there was a twinkle in those kiddish eyes of his. You know, and there was a lot of vitality in his movements. He used to wear him out. You know, we only played the two nights a week. It was his club, and he could call the shots as he wished. And business, I think, was such that he was wise. He stayed open on Friday and Saturday nights only. Didn't have to worry about bartender payrolls and all that sort of thing during the early part of the week when you would have died. And then the gamble is, do you make the money on the weekend or not? Well, he gambled, I'll stay open on the weekend only, and if we make it, we make it. You know, and it's a little more profit. I think that was probably good sound business. So we played the Friday and the Saturday nights. And by Saturday nights, he was pretty tired. Because he always gave. You know, he didn't hold back. He really played. Those choruses that you hear on the records, which I consider very carefully crafted works of musical art, they're his creations. I have no idea whether he worked them out in his head at some point in history, or if indeed he wrote them down at some point in history, memorized the concept, and then went with it. But he played his material just about the same every time. On a given tune, whether it be an oldie like Tiger Rag, or a simple basic old, old tune like Careless Love, or a fairly contemporary pop tune, or a hokum like Wabash Blues, things like that, which he'd play. Played it about the same. But he wasn't grinding it out in a perfunctory way. No, it was played, you know, with some guts. It really came from down. It had vitality. And at this point in time in 1975, I'm disappointed that none of the trombonists I've heard in New Orleans are playing with any kind of gut-level vitality. They're playing a little bit superficially. They're playing notes. They're playing notes. But playing jazz, the Laori conceived it. I was playing more than notes. You're playing a lot of raw emotion. And I like that. A lot of people can play Carnival of Venice and Flight of the Bumblebee. It's not very moving. Play a nice, simple, gutty chorus on something like Pagan Love Song. It can be a really nice musical experience. I think I learned in my first trip to New Orleans an important thing. In New Orleans music, it's not the name of the tune, but it's how you play any tune. Name me something off the hit parade. You know, that's saying, well, that dates me, doesn't it? Hit parade. But you just take something out of the pop milieu, and you play it in good, honest New Orleans style, then I think you've got an understanding of New Orleans music.
We were talking earlier, and I'd like to get you placed in your age and everything. When's your birthday?

Oh, it comes in September every year, whether I want it to or not. Born in 1926. My college years, grew up in California. My college years started 1943. I had to go in the Navy in 45, 46, then got back to college and started chasing people like Kid Horry, because I was a pretty serious jazz record collector by that time, and spent a lot of time trying to soak up the music. I had taken cornet lessons when I was nine years old. Never was very distinguished. The school music teacher would always put me in the farthest back row in the very last chair and hoped that I wouldn't show up. Later on, though, there was something in me that wanted to come out, and I started playing on my own. I never could read music. I could barely spell music, as the expression goes. I can point to the note, and I'll tell you what it is, but that's as far as it goes. But I started trying to translate what I was hearing on these recordings and from these good musicians that I was able to hear like Horry. I found that I could turn around and reproduce it to a degree. And that's how it all started.
Who else did you hear live other than Horry's band? Who else did you hear? Who else did you hear?

In Los Angeles in those days, there was a guy named Pete Daly out of Chicago-style Dixieland band. He was quite good. Clareness, Rosie McHarg. It's a long time since I really thought about those people. I never was fond of playing that way. I found myself in New York in the 50s, 50 to 55, playing alongside an incredible roster of musicians. This was in the days with the Conrad Janus band. Conrad Janus on the Tailgate Five, he called it. It was a five-piece group usually. But we'd play alongside just about the who's who of jazz, really. We'd see Henry Red Allen all the time, Willie the Lion Smith, Jonah Jones would come by and scare everybody to death, people like Buster Bailey, fine clarinetist. I did have a chance to play with Earl Father Hines in San Francisco. I had a way of lucking out when trumpet players would get sick and I'd get called. I never felt badly about being second choice because I think I would have chosen those other guys first too. There was a trumpet player named Eddie Smith working for Father Hines in San Francisco. He was very good. But he got sick for a couple weeks and I was able to play with the band, which included Darnell Howard, another New Orleans legend. I thought he was just delightful to work with, a beautiful person. I met a new Albert Nicholas in New York. I remember having dinner with him at a restaurant. He was a very elegant gentleman, loved his fine food, and he was as meticulous as his clarinet playing sounds. He was just a really fine and polished gentleman. And, of course, some of the younger people, Dick Wellstead was very close. We played in the Janus Band for a couple of years together. Chad sits. I'm not doing too well on free recall. Well, I've got a lot of questions. You name him and I've rubbed elbows. I remember Muggsy Spanier hated to play alongside the Count Rajanis Band because we always played loud and rowdy and the crowd liked it. Muggsy was growing old gracefully and played wonderful. Muggsy was a very strong early influence. I had those old Bluebird, Muggsy Spanier and the Ragtimers. I learned a lot of basic things. Of course, George Brunis was on those.
What else? Could you tell me that story again about Zutty? About Zutty? If that's worth telling again. Oh, I...

About Zutty and Red Island for what it says. I thought it... Well, I just thought it was amusing. It about fell off the bandstand. This was at one of the jazz jam session halls where maybe two bands would get together to jam a little bit at the end of each set, you know. It was kind of a nice life. Each band played half an hour. Half hour on, half hour off, which is certainly not going to kill you. And it was good for the crowd because they got continuous live vital music. But the Janus Band was on the bill plus Henry Red Allen and Willie the Lion Smith, Zutty Singleton, probably Saul Yegud, and I just don't remember who all. Probably Big Chief Russell Moore or somebody like that playing from home. Or it could have been Wilbur DeParis. It could have been Sandy Williams. It could have been a lot of people like that. Herb Fleming would have been another possible. But Zutty had a way of playing that was sort of down home. Very meticulous. See, he played on the beat. He played right in the middle of the beat. Zutty did not push the beat. He did not ride lightly on the cymbals. He was not bouncing along ahead of you, no. He was playing some press rolls and some good fundamental right on the beat. Well, this has a tendency to perhaps slow things down. And on this one occasion, I do believe Zutty was slowing down. Now, that might have been that he was doing it to be perverse because some of the other members of the band were kind of goosing it and moving ahead. But in the middle of this conflict and concepts of tempo, Henry Redd Allen just turned around and looked at Zutty and he says, Man, don't you all stop! And, you know, all the musicians, nobody else knew what that was about. But Zutty was just playing so dead flat in the middle and, well, it was bugging Henry Redd Allen. He was a bit of a powerhouse character. He was a great entertainer. He would really take charge. He could really rock a whole hall. The hall I'm talking about was the Central Plaza in New York, which was active at least in my years from 50 to 55 and probably a little longer after that. Every weekend they'd have that continuous music policy in a huge room on the Lower East Side. Must have held 600, 700 people. Beer by the pitcher for a dollar, dollar and a quarter. Buck to get in. He did all right.
They drew the people, apparently.
Yeah, they had good people. I'm sorry I'm not doing better on Free Recall. I could name you names.
I mean, the crowd. There must have been a good-sized crowd.

Oh, a good-sized crowd. Yeah, lots of fans in those days. The so-called Dixieland was quite a big thing. This is pre-Elvis Presley. Pre-rock. In fact, I was living and working in New York when Alan Freed came out of, I think it was Cleveland, to break it up in New York and he came into town using the name Moondog, which had been his radio name in Cleveland. And then the real Moondog, the street musician, promptly sued him and won. So Alan Freed had to just become Alan Freed and then he went on to be rock promoter and that kind of thing and make some of those early 50s rock movies and, you know, associated with the era of Bill Haley and the Comets and that kind of thing. But Dixieland was very big until it got kind of wiped out by the ad net of rock. I forgot to ask you
who was in the Ori band.

At the time, I was in the Ori band and we're talking again the 1958 to 60 era. Boy, I'm about to draw a blank on the piano player, which was terrible. Let's see. Well, anyway, the front line was Ori, of course, trombone. I was playing trumpet. The clarinetist was either Bill Shea or Ellis Horn, who had been a veteran of the Lou Waters band. Bill Napier, for a short while, right before he went east to join Bob Scobie for one of Scobie's last major trips. Napier was very good, fit the band very well. And back of us, we had Bobby Ozobin, a very good drummer who had the opposite of Zutty, had a nice light touch, did indeed swing very well. And the Ori band just did not require an overpowering drummer because Ori played an ensemble driving tightness that was in itself a force and you didn't have to have volume to go along with it. And you could play very comfortably with the band and still have a lot of punch, you know, everybody's playing together and Bobby Ozobin fit very well with that group. He'd done some traveling, I know, with Ivory Joe Hunter in the 50s. I don't know what other groups. He was a California musician. That's really funny. I just can't think who the piano player might have been. We may have to turn the tape off
while I think that. No, we'll come to you.
We probably had a bass player and I can't think who that was right now.
Well, I hope the piano player played good chords.

Oh, I hope so because I certainly needed that because I didn't name chords by name but I sure relied on them to play on top of my own, what little ability I had, my intuitive and playing by ear. I could sure tell a bad chord when I heard it and I would get really frozen up if I heard a bad one coming at me. But if I heard good chords and some good rhythm, I sounded indeed better than I was. I'm just sorry I never had a chance to record with the Ori band but he did not do any recording in that period.

There was several piano players out there that I think about. Like, I don't suppose you ever knew Lionel Reason. No, I don't remember that name. He lived in California for a while and he was with Ori and, well, previously he'd been with King Oliver. No, he'd been way back. Way back.
In the 30s and I knew him down here
and I understand he's back in Baton Rouge.

My favorite piano player in San Francisco and she is still there and still active is Jack's sister, Norma Teagarden. I find her just a delightful player and a delightful person and her abilities just encompass everything. She can literally play everything from the classics to the rags very well and she can just, if I may be so indelicate, she can just swing her ass off. She's just a wonderful player. Just a delightful, vital force in any kind of a group. I always look forward to playing with her.
It's funny that she's never made more of a name for herself. She's not a pushy

kind of person and she would not require the roar of the crowd. She always delighted in the fact that her brother Jack was so famous. She always will tell you that their mother was the great musician in the family, the great teacher of them all. She was very proud of her brother Charlie Teagarden, the trumpet player. She had a brother that she called Cub. I believe his name was Clovis Teagarden. He went off to go straight in the business world at some point but he was apparently a pretty good drummer. So it was all in all quite a family. Indeed.
Well, who was with Ori when you were going out in your college days?

Well, Buster Wilson was on the piano and Ed Garland, Montutti was with him in the minor hall and Bud Scott. I even heard Bud Scott. I don't think I ever heard Mutt Carey but I did hear people like Andrew Blakeney who I thought very highly of and I remember being in a club called the Beverly Cavern in Los Angeles the night that Teddy Buckner first joined the Ori band. Now, Teddy's a fine horn player. No, no question. He really is a good man. He can really get around but he showed up this first time. He had his trumpet. He later converted to cornet for a little softer sound but he had the trumpet that he'd been playing with the Lionel Hampton group and things like that and he was playing a pretty strident kind of horn and it didn't really fit the Ori style exactly and some of us who were sort of loyal Ori followers were bothered a little bit by this. I remember I came up with a very uncomplimentary name for Teddy which I sincerely regret. I called him My God who's that Bill Screamo or something like that because he was really kind of screaming a bit because that was his immediate background but it wasn't long. It wasn't very darn many weeks before Ori did like to rehearse. He didn't for the little two day a week thing but Ori did like to rehearse and keep his bands sharp and drag out some of the more complicated things some of the tunes that had three and four strains of different keys but it wasn't long before Teddy Buckner was just playing a very nice horn and he shifted to cornet for a softer sound and that of course was a relationship that lasted quite a while.
Well when you were with Ori did you say you didn't rehearse much with him? Did you rehearse No

I only tried rehearsing a couple of different times and I forget what the occasion was he just wanted to get a couple of tunes out I can remember rehearsing Memphis Blues with him I think probably the band was such a natural he could have just played it right off as a sort of a scholarly approach myself you know I knew all the strains to it he just could have agreed to a structure and played it
did you play any of the complicated numbers oh
let me think we used to yeah we used to play maple leaf rag tiger rag Memphis blues
mostly
the audience at that time was not all that historically minded they just liked good music they didn't really care what the tune was and they indeed did like Max the knife
did they make many requests

yeah yeah I don't know what trumpet player was started it but I used to have to play sugar blues which I hated to do never liked to duplicate somebody else's material and I didn't feel a very strong affinity for it but we'd have to play things like that you mean with the mute
is that what you're talking about that type of sugar blues

yeah I don't think I didn't do that I played it I can remember hearing a very tasteful recording years ago by Buck Clayton Buck Clayton and Don Bias little quartet or quintet recording of sugar blues which they just played it very straightforward and honestly and I think that influenced me and I think I preferred to play it that way which of course would be a great disappointment to an audience that wanted to hear a lot of wah-wah rickety-tick razzmatazz things like things like Wabash Blues would come up well you know Ori would play the lead on that and do a little hokum that's fine you know audiences like that and after all you're playing for them I feel sorry for musicians who can only play for themselves it must be a fairly lonesome life
did you have any idols when you were coming up

oh yeah I um it's funny I sort of worked backwards in my um taste I was first attracted to Harry James he played you know fantastic trumpet player let's face it man played brilliantly and I thought that was really great and then I heard uh those Muggsy Spanier records that I mentioned the ragtimers and I thought wow this is a whole different thing and I liked that and then finally I worked my way back to uh some Louis Armstrong and the Hot Five and Hot Seven things like that really liked those and then started getting back earlier to King Oliver and then I started hearing some of what I'd have to call the New Orleans primitives some of the people who never left the city and played how one might imagine a neighborhood band might have played in 1910 and I learned to really appreciate that kind of thing and as I got farther and farther back into the roots then I found it easier for me to understand the music and then begin to construct my own style on top of that and I always used to be annoyed when little little phrases or things from say Harry James or Muxi Spanier might pop into my playing you know it's pretty hard not to pick up other people's cliches I was never I was never very fond of Vicks Beiderbeck I never wanted to play like Vicks Beiderbeck I can listen to him and really enjoy what he's doing but it's kind of like watching Charlie Chaplin movies I watch them without laughing I appreciate what he's doing but he's not my man like W.C. Fields is or the March Brothers are I don't know if that parallel makes any sense but I just he was Beiderbeck was just over there and I appreciated what he was doing but I didn't ever want to play like that I just really was more attracted to what I felt was a simpler more honest approach to swing and jazz music out of whatever the tune might happen to be and I appreciated the lesson of coming to New Orleans and finding out that jazz is how you play something off the current hit parade which in 1950 my first visit happened to be Mona Lisa or Jambalaya tunes like that and I was able to hear the bands and the roadhouses that you took me to hear playing those tunes it was a revelation
who did we go to hear oh we went

to Lutchen's to hear Billy and D.D. Pierce remember them very vividly I can remember going to hear Emil Barnes really appreciated his music trombonist a little guy named Harrison Brazley I was brash enough to ask to sit in mention some tune I asked him if he knew it and he says you play it I'll trombone for you and he did he was right I was a dumb kid
well even the best ones sometimes get confused when they have to change keys things like that they're not used to playing something in a
key
yeah
that's true
I've seen that happen to Jimmy Darcy who must have had every kind of experience imaginable as a young man and playing and he couldn't get together with the Dukes of Dixon and he had any kind of keys

now that's odd because even my limited experience we always played in all kinds of keys with the Conrad Janus band just for exercise we used to deliberately change keys or transpose in the middle of tunes just to you get a very different flavor out of a tune when you play it in a different key because I can't explain how it happens but you just get a very different feeling I tell you you get in a very difficult key you start playing in D flat
you're

going to start playing a little bit simpler to begin with and you might kind of get on a more basic driving thing because your fingers just aren't glib in that key the more you play in it of course the more you're going to be glib but you're going to be glib in that key and a lot of the patterns that are going to come out are going to be very different than if you were playing in E flat or B flat easier trumpet keys
we've been listening to Raymond Burke did you hear him when you came down here

yes I did the recordings I heard today I thought were just very good and a good deal smoother than I remember Raymond Raymond had a good rough rough edge to his playing when I heard him which I happen to like I prefer that well I like I like all styles I think
in California who did you play with did we cover that when you

started well it was just an amateur band there was a band that put together with clarinetist Tom Sharpstein and Conrad Janis was the trombone player and some other people we cut a little disc in a basketball court one night at some high school in Glendale and mailed it into the record changer magazine they were having their first annual amateur jazz band contest our band won I think we sent in a crude recording of Canal Street Blues and maybe Snake Rag something like that very King Oliver oriented at that time and we won and then nothing much happened until a number of years later they sold the record most of mine
they sold the record over the
panel I think so could be
nothing much
happened nothing much happened in California because my next musical experiences all happened in New York 1950 to 55 I guess the date of entering that contest must have been 48 or 49 yeah

we could sure check that out because I remember that I remember hearing the record and I think it was on their own label I still have the books in which I kept all sort of an inventory book that I kept I kept a list of everything in the record shop on the different labels and probably have that one listed

and then back out to San Francisco I played for a short while with the Turk Murphy band and then he went on the road for a long period and I had a I had by the time I had a wife and a fairly newborn child and so I wanted to put down a root so I did I stayed there and worked in the record business wholesale records luckily jazz records so I could do a meaningful job in selling that kind of material I was able to play with the George Lewis band for a few weeks in 1957 as I recall his trumpet player at the time was Thomas Jefferson and for some reason he wanted to come running home to New Orleans which he did very abruptly

segments.title: Smith's full name
segments.summary: He explains he was named Richard Charles Howard Smith to distinguish him among relatives.

segments.title: Playing in Kid Ory's band: style, Sheik of Araby, Mack the Knife
segments.summary: Smith recalls following Ory's band in college, then playing trumpet in it on weekends; describes Ory's ensemble style, opener and favorite tunes.

segments.title: Ory's theme song and his age
segments.summary: Ory's sentimental closing theme 'Without You, For an Inspiration, Dear', and talk of Ory being about 75 yet personable.

segments.title: Ory's weekend club, consistent playing, and New Orleans way with tunes
segments.summary: Ory ran the club two nights a week, played his crafted choruses the same each time with real vitality; Smith contrasts this with superficial modern trombonists and says New Orleans music is how you play any tune.

segments.chapter: Early life and New York years
segments.title: Birth, college, Navy and learning to play by ear
segments.summary: Born 1926 in California, he took cornet lessons at nine, served in the Navy, collected records, and taught himself to play by ear.

segments.chapter: Early life and New York years
segments.title: Hearing live bands and playing in New York with the Conrad Janis band
segments.summary: He lists Los Angeles bands he heard, then musicians met in New York with Janis's Tailgate Five, Hines in San Francisco, and Muggsy Spanier's influence.

segments.chapter: Early life and New York years
segments.title: Zutty Singleton and Red Allen at the Central Plaza
segments.summary: Story of Zutty's on-the-beat drumming irritating Red Allen at New York's Central Plaza, with a description of the hall.

segments.chapter: Early life and New York years
segments.title: Dixieland crowds, Alan Freed and the rise of rock
segments.summary: Crowds were large before rock; Alan Freed's Moondog episode and Dixieland's decline.

segments.chapter: Kid Ory band personnel and repertoire
segments.title: Personnel of the Ory band, 1958-60
segments.summary: Front line, drummer Bobby Ozobin, forgotten piano and bass players, and the importance of good chords.

segments.chapter: Kid Ory band personnel and repertoire
segments.title: Lionel Reason and other Ory pianists
segments.summary: The interviewer asks about pianist Lionel Reason, whom Smith doesn't recall.

segments.chapter: Kid Ory band personnel and repertoire
segments.title: Norma Teagarden and the Teagarden family
segments.summary: Smith praises San Francisco pianist Norma Teagarden and describes her musical family.

segments.chapter: Kid Ory band personnel and repertoire
segments.title: Ory's earlier band and Teddy Buckner joining
segments.summary: Musicians Smith heard with Ory in his college days, and the night Teddy Buckner first joined.

segments.chapter: Kid Ory band personnel and repertoire
segments.title: Rehearsals and repertoire with Ory
segments.summary: Rarely rehearsed; tunes included Maple Leaf Rag, Tiger Rag, Memphis Blues, and Mack the Knife for a non-historical audience.

segments.title: Audience requests and playing Sugar Blues
segments.summary: He disliked copying others' material like Sugar Blues, preferring a straight Buck Clayton approach, and defends playing for the audience.

segments.title: Musical idols and working backward to New Orleans roots
segments.summary: From Harry James to Spanier, Armstrong, Oliver and New Orleans primitives; not fond of Beiderbecke; first New Orleans visit in 1950.

segments.title: Hearing New Orleans bands on the 1950 visit
segments.summary: Roadhouse visits to hear Billie and De De Pierce, Emile Barnes, and sitting in with a trombonist.

segments.title: Changing keys and playing in difficult keys
segments.summary: Discussion of musicians struggling with key changes; Smith's Janis band transposed deliberately and he explains how difficult keys alter playing.

segments.title: Raymond Burke's playing
segments.summary: Smith comments on recordings of Raymond Burke, smoother than he remembered but with a rough edge he liked.

segments.title: California amateur band and Record Changer contest
segments.summary: Amateur band with Tom Sharpstein and Conrad Janis won a Record Changer contest with a recording; nothing else came of it in California.

segments.title: Back in San Francisco: Turk Murphy, record business, George Lewis
segments.summary: After New York he played briefly with Turk Murphy, settled into wholesale jazz records, and played with George Lewis in 1957.
